import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 452

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/452](https://www.erdosproblems.com/452)
-/

namespace Erdos452

open scoped ArithmeticFunction.omega

/-- The greatest length of an interval in $[x,2x]$ on which
$\omega(n) > \log\log n$ everywhere. -/
noncomputable def largeOmegaIntervalLength (x : ℕ) : ℕ := by
  classical
  exact Nat.findGreatest
    (fun len ↦ ∃ start, x ≤ start ∧ start + len ≤ 2 * x + 1 ∧
      ∀ n ∈ Finset.Ico start (start + len),
        Real.log (Real.log (n : ℝ)) < (ω n : ℝ))
    (x + 1)

/-- Determine the largest length of an interval in $[x,2x]$ on which
$\omega(n) > \log\log n$ everywhere. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_452 : largeOmegaIntervalLength = answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

end Erdos452

reformulations.difference: The source’s largest integer interval inside [x,2x] is represented by a half-open interval Finset.Ico start (start + len), with endpoint bound start + len ≤ 2*x + 1 and a bounded Nat.findGreatest search.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For len > 0, this is exactly the closed integer interval [start,start+len−1], has cardinality len, and lies in [x,2x]. Conversely, any nonempty closed integer interval [a,b] inside [x,2x] is represented with start=a and len=b+1−a. Every admissible length is at most x+1, so the search bound excludes nothing. Length zero is always admissible, so Nat.findGreatest’s fallback does not create a spurious maximum. The interval correspondence and maximum characterization were proved in /workspace/review/verification.lean.

reformulations.difference: The answer is a single function of type ℕ → ℕ, specified by function equality, rather than a pointwise statement with an explicit parameter x.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For every candidate function f, largeOmegaIntervalLength = f is equivalent to saying, for every x, that f x is an admissible length and every admissible length is at most f x. This follows from function extensionality and the proved maximum characterization. The full equivalence was checked in Lean; the answer is genuinely constrained, not arbitrary.

review.notes: Both declarations were checked. The cited source still records the problem as OPEN; its July 2026 discussion supplies only a proposed partial upper bound. Lean verification established f(0)=0, f(1)=1, and f(2)=3, and confirmed that ω counts distinct prime factors. The logarithm’s exceptional values affect only the small-input extension; for x≥2 every tested integer is in the usual logarithm domain.
